overview: A two-page consular despatch from Dairen reports plans for a network of thirteen powerful aviation beacons across Manchuria and describes recent military air maneuvers over the Kwantung Leased Territory. American Consul Stuart E. Grummon notes that the first beacon was planned near the Dairen airport at Choushuitzu and the second near Wafangtien, under a program sponsored by the Employees Association of the South Manchuria Railway Company. He also reports bombing practice and low-altitude stunt flying by military aircraft, most of them dispatched from Heijo in Korea.

subfiles.title: Despatch from Grummon on new air beacons and air maneuvers
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports plans for aviation beacons in Manchuria and military air maneuvers over the Kwantung Leased Territory.
subfiles.summary: Grummon reports a press announcement that a four-thousand-candlepower beacon would be erected near Choushuitzu, the Dairen airport, as the first of thirteen beacons intended to support night flying throughout Manchuria. A second beacon was planned near Wafangtien, and the program was sponsored by the Employees Association of the South Manchuria Railway Company. He also describes April 17–19 air maneuvers over Chinchow, Dairen, and Port Arthur involving about thirty aircraft, mostly from Heijo in Korea, including live bombing of a wooden target and dangerous low-altitude stunt flying over Dairen. Copies were distributed to the Department and American diplomatic and consular offices in Peiping, Tokyo, Mukden, Harbin, and Shanghai.

interest: The despatch links civilian aviation infrastructure with conspicuous military air activity in Japanese-controlled Manchuria, making it useful for studying the overlap between transportation development, colonial administration, and military preparedness. Its contrast between the initially reported 200 aircraft and the roughly thirty actually observed offers evidence about contemporary press claims and consular verification. The details about live bombing and hazardous low-altitude flying also provide a vivid local account of Japanese military aviation in the Kwantung Leased Territory in 1935.
